game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Let me start with saying this: 
This game is creepy AF, if you think about it deeply. Orwell was right, even in 1948 (or 1984, depends on how you want to look at it).

Initially you're searching for details about Oleg Bakay, a missing military officer from neighboring country Parges. Soon--and for the remainder of the game--your focus shifts to Raban Vhart, a blogger whose anti-government sentiments and campaign against the leadership of The Nation (which is, yes, run by a man who looks a bit like Trump) must be thwarted. You are, essentially, the bad guy, running surveillance for a dictatorship that demands absolute fealty from the citizens it so closely monitors, but Ignorance is Strength is less explicit about the meaning behind all of this than the first game was. While Orwell stretched across five episodic instalments, Ignorance is Strength runs for just three, which winds up being too little time to build upon the previously established mythology of the game's world. The broader political climate of The Nation, the appropriately Orwellian setting for both games, isn't expanded upon much by Raban's war against it, and while a conflict with Parges is discussed it's never quite explored enough to feel like a proper plot point.

Your job is to find chunks of data online using the computer interface of the Orwell surveillance system, then throw as much dirt as you can at Raban. If a piece of information on a page can be collected, it will be highlighted, and you can drag it to their profile on your screen. You find this information by scouring websites (although annoyingly you can't "search" for sites; you either find links on sites you have already accessed or gain a new site for your database after grabbing a data chunk), and when you manage to find someone's phone or computer details you can snoop through their private screens too. Pages that haven't been fully explored, or which have data chunks you haven't lifted, are highlighted on your list of pages visited. Each piece of information you collect will eat up ten minutes on your in-game clock, and in each of the game's three episodes you're working towards a specific time limit, so you want to focus on the important information and skip over any data that does not add to the case you're building.

Sometimes data will contradict with other chunks, and as the Investigator it's up to you to choose which one to submit. The "Ethical Codex" mandate means that your supervisor is only privy to information you submit, and will make informed decisions based on that. The way the plot progresses will be influenced by which statements you decide are more valid, as you can't submit two contradictory pieces. It's an implausible system, but from a game design perspective it's a clever one, forcing you into regular moral dilemmas.

As you read through the information, the Orwell system will highlight relevant passages of text as data chunks. The system itself is incredibly literal, and unable to distinguishes nuances of language. It can't, for instance, tell that, by listing their current location as 'The Internet', your target is making a funny joke. In fact, if Orwell was analysing that last sentence, it would offer a data chunk saying I thought putting 'The Internet' as your location is a funny joke. It doesn't do sarcasm.

The obvious limitation is that you can't make recommendations. Your ability to control and shape the situation comes from the data you do or, often more crucially, don't upload. Orwell teaches this lesson early on, when a target jokes about stealing her boyfriend's credit card. Upload that data chunk and Symes, who can't see the playful dynamic of the relationship, has the card cancelled. In later episodes, the stakes are more dramatic. There are some major decisions that can have a profound effect on the story—albeit, as is often the case with episodic storytelling, the story follows the same major beats no matter your choices. But doing what seems like the noble thing doesn't always lead to the best outcome. It's complicated and messy, which feels right.

Despite these problems, Orwell is a success. It lets you watch over a spiralling conspiratorial thriller, and throws in enough twists and surprises to keep things interesting. It's an enjoyable way to interact with a world—the voyeurism creating a distinct, enjoyable power dynamic that I refuse to self-reflect on any further. It's not at all subtle—it's called Orwell, after all—but it's a well told mystery framed by a captivating storytelling device.

The story telling was amazing, tho a bit too *I am waiting for an animation to skip* 
It was fun, but definitely deserves to be played with time and clear mind. 
Now if you will excuse me, I will try to disconnect from Orwell

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
The technology displayed in Orwell is already out there, though it's not called Orwell. And it's much more sophisticated. Whether you're a government agency, an intelligence agency or just someone powerful who has the ability to tap into the right resources, the data are out there. Government records, bank records, phone tracking, social media, internet activity, etc. It's already here and it's not that hard to piece together. Obviously, this is just a game, so it's perfectly understandable why Orwell isn't as sophisticated.

So, we live in a very terrifying world, it seems... but this game actually made me realise it's not as grim as it looks like. The concepts and warnings of this game, given the state of our society and the in-game characters, actually fall flat and, like I said, make you realise it's not that bad. Was that the intention, I wonder.

Why? Well, the majority of the monitored characters are either massive jerks (Cassandra and Harrison) or dangerous and certainly deserving investigation (I've already spoiled too much). And investigation isn't necessarily a bad thing. Even before the information age, there were detectives and police officers investigating crimes and stuff. The thing is about finding the right balance, I guess, but that's out of the scope if this game and its message.

Before this game, these things always worried me and I always thought about the impact on us all. Innocents caught and crushed between the merciless cogs of surveillance and false illusion of freedom. However, I failed to take into account that it's not just those behind those tools that are jerks. It's also those who end up between those cogs. So hey, maybe it's not so grim after all.

Like that line in the 1984 book about imagining the future -- a boot stamping on a human face, forever. If that face belongs to a jerk, then it's actually kinda good. True, innocent people will still get caught between the cogs, but at least it's not 100% just innocents. It probably is more like just 10% of the time. Cool. Thank you, Orwell, I guess I can sleep better at night today. :)

Honestly, this is one of the best games I have ever played.

Similar to Papers, Please, this game is about a government worker who is entrusted with determining the danger level of certain individuals in order to keep the world safe. Is that what they are really doing?

The characters in this game are all very distinct, with unique personalities and behaviours. You feel their pain and their joy. One character in particular I felt much pain for when some of his secrets were revealed. He was as much a victim as the others.

This game is a truly wonderous experience, with a different format than any other game I've ever played.

If you're a fan of an immersive story and dystopian elements, there is no game I would recommend more than Orwell. 

I am greatly looking forward to the sequel!

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw: Orwell is basically just working but with more steps. Thankfully I got it on sale, but I wouldn’t recommend it as I felt I was just doing admin work the whole time. Osmotic Studios, a small German indie team, made this 2016 surveillance thriller where you play as a government agent using the Orwell system to dig through people’s emails, chats, social media, and documents after some incidents in a fictional country that feels a lot like a modern Western nation. You highlight and upload data, make choices about what goes into official reports, and watch the consequences play out. There’s a sequel too (Ignorance is Strength), which I've read is the same basic formula. Now the concept is clever on paper, digital Big Brother stuff inspired by the real world, and the writing tries to be thoughtful about privacy versus security.What I didn’t like: the actual gameplay is almost entirely reading walls of text, clicking highlighted bits, and filing them away. It starts feeling like busywork pretty fast, scrolling through inboxes, profiles, and logs for the next piece of info to stamp and upload. The interface is clean and the story has some twists, but the loop never evolves much beyond do your paperwork. It can drag, and the moral dilemmas lose punch when the moment-to-moment experience is so dry and repetitive. Not much in the way of challenge or variety either.If you must play it, stick to PC where it runs fine and the mouse and keyboard setup suits the desktop-sim style. Overall though, not for me. 4/10.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell is for players who like investigation and mystery. If you don't enjoy extensive reading, you're not going to have fun. However, if you love researching bits of evidence across numerous faux websites, phone conversations, text messages, emails, and more, this is the game for you. The opportunities to spy on everyone and everything quickly become unnervingly attractive.

One catch: Orwell has multiple endings and the story can go a number of different ways, but progression can feel frustratingly limited at times. While the player does have the freedom to decide which evidence to submit/ignore, they are often required to stick to a specific list in order to move forward. However, the upside to this is that progression is nearly always intuitive. 

While not perfect, Orwell allows players to become an omniscient government agent who can truly see all, using formidable tools to influence a nation. I highly recommend this game with a solid 8/10 rating.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
This is a visual novel along the same lines as A Lost Phone. Everything you might want to click is almost always highlighted with a red box, star, or a red/blue/grey page icon by the resource's entry in your listing, so getting lost and missing things is tricky. The main challenge is deciding what to submit as evidence and what not to. In my first playthrough, I submitted everything I found, just to see what it did, but in later playthroughs I was more discerning, shaping the narrative to my own ends.

The story is a fairly good one about omnipresent surveillance, though unlikely to give chills to anyone who knows the NSA exists. The system in the game is *ridiculously* hobbled compared to real-world ones: they can only spy on people they have permission to; they can only view documents and devices that have been revealed through the investigation; they can't communicate; they can't correct any ambiguities with better information; they can't... etc etc. It's a deliberately-hobbled system, for reasons made clear during the game, but it does have the advantage that, technologically at least, they have access to *everything, immediately*.

All possible endings are morally ambivalent, so there's arguably no "good" or "bad" ending.

While there's an option to speed up phone calls and messaging, it only works a little bit, speeding it up from "interminable crawl" to "this is bearable, but still painful to replay". There are some minor bugs about the highlighting of things, particularly where mouseovering things doesn't always show the tooltip describing its effects. But the tooltips aren't critical, you can guess from context.

100%-ing the achievements it is a bit of a pain for completionists, since you have to play through it 2.5 times, but it's entirely possible, and the game repays another playthrough or two because there are multiple endings and outcomes for most of the characters, depending whether you play pro-government, pro-activist, or somewhere between.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I'm surprised how lukewarm a lot of the reviews of this game are - I thought it was phenomenal! I guess it's because the game is mostly reading?

The government has created a piece of software designed to spy on anyone and everyone with the aim of catching criminals and terrorists. You are recruited as an investigator tasked with using it to create profiles of suspicious individuals, going through their emails, phones, desktops, etc... aiming to find anything incriminating.

Although it might seem obvious that an all-powerful piece of spying software may be somewhat unethical, Orwell does a great job at making you [i]experience[/i] it. When you're listening in on a suspect's phone call and rather than anything incriminating you just hear an argument between a couple going through a hard time in their relationship, you feel kinda gross. When you label somebody as angry and hateful based on a blog post they wrote years ago, which you later found out they regret, you get a pit in your stomach realising that the profile you made of them could have a big negative impact on this person's life in the future.

Saying that, the game doesn't feel preachy. You [i]are[/i] able to use the software to hunt down and reveal criminals who may have otherwise gone scot-free, and the game makes it clear that increased surveillance [i]is[/i] leading to dramatic reductions in crime. So does that make the gross invasion of privacy ultimately justified?? I really enjoyed how conflicted I felt up to the very end and how much it made me think.

This is a game where your choices really do matter, different people may live, die, or be arrested in your playthrough based on the choices that you make. I actually replayed the final chapter a second time because I wasn't satisfied with my ending, and managed to unlock a lot of extra information I didn't get the first time. 

I was super gripped the whole way through and am excited to play the sequel now!
